# pandas

Python's in-memory dataframe library. In [[labour-fraud-analysis]] it carries the entire analytical
argument — and, notably, **nothing else**.

## The boundary: pandas at the surface, stdlib `csv` in the pipeline

Verified from the import graph across all eight `src/` modules plus the notebook and the test suite:

| Uses pandas | Uses the standard-library `csv` module |
|---|---|
| `src/app.py` — the [[streamlit]] dashboard | `anonymize.py`, `build_db.py`, `build_docs.py`, `build_viewer.py`, `port_report.py`, `validate_anonymization.py` |
| `notebooks/01_investigation_analysis.ipynb` | `src/tests/test_dataset.py` |

The anonymisation pipeline, the SQLite build, the generated docs, the [[disclosure-gate]] and the
whole test suite are written against `csv.DictReader` and `collections.Counter`. That is a real and
defensible split rather than an inconsistency: the pipeline's job is faithful row-by-row
transformation of untrusted text where a dataframe's type inference is a liability, and the analysis
surface's job is fast grouped aggregation where it is the point. The test suite staying on stdlib
also means the integrity checks do not depend on the library whose behaviour they would otherwise be
testing through.

## The two idioms that carry everything

**Read everything as text, coerce per analysis.**

```python
pd.read_csv(path, dtype=str).fillna("")           # every table, every column
pd.to_numeric(df["value"], errors="coerce")       # only where a number is needed
```

Nothing is inferred at load time. A permit number that looks like an integer stays a string; a
contract value becomes numeric only inside the one analysis that needs it, with unparseable rows
becoming `NaN` rather than raising. For a forensic dataset that deliberately retains data-quality
artefacts — OCR-mangled dates are kept, not cleaned — this is the correct default: type inference
would quietly "fix" exactly the damage the dataset exists to exhibit.

**Group, count, sort.** Every one of the four named signals is one of:

- `groupby([date, employer]).size()` — bulk sponsorship batches
- `value_counts()` on a contact column — [[shared-identifier-clustering]]
- a 30-bin histogram of a coerced numeric column — declared-wage uniformity
- `groupby([year, employer]).size()` — entity succession

No statistical model, no significance test, no outlier score. The method is aggregation plus
[[convergent-evidence]]; pandas is exactly sized for it.

## In the dashboard

The whole `data/csv` directory is loaded into a `dict[str, DataFrame]` behind `@st.cache_data`, so
twenty tables are parsed once per session. Frames feed plotly figures directly and the graph
analysis via [[networkx]]; the notebook plots the same frames through [[matplotlib]] instead. Both
recompute from the CSVs on every run — nothing is hard-coded, see [[reproducible-analysis]].
